title: readonly, Readonly<T>, and immutability flags
hook: The readonly keyword tells TypeScript that a property or array should not be mutated after creation — a compile-time promise, not a runtime lock.

blocks.text: **readonly** marks properties and arrays as not assignable after initialization. **`Readonly<T>`** shallowly freezes every property. **`readonly` arrays** disallow push/pop. Immutability is **compile-time only** — JavaScript objects stay mutable unless you copy or freeze. C# offers stronger run-time contracts with init accessors and immutable collections.

entries.plainDefinition: Prevents reassignment after construction. Shallow only.
Maps every property of T to readonly.
Top-level readonly; nested objects may still mutate.
entries.example: Readonly<{ inner: { x: number } }> — inner.x can change.

blocks.text: React/Angular benefit from readonly props. Reducers should return new state. Mutable arrays assign to readonly parameters, not reverse.

blocks.title: Compile-time only
blocks.body: readonly emits nothing. Use Object.freeze or Immer for real immutability.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming deep immutability. Expecting runtime protection. Passing readonly array where mutable T[] required.

blocks.text: Deep immutability needs recursive mapped types or Immer. C# record with expressions provides copy semantics TS lacks natively.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Claiming readonly enforces runtime immutability. Not knowing shallow vs deep.

interviewTakeaways: as const produces readonly literal tuples.
60s: Compile-time shallow flag. Immer for nested. C# init/records stronger at runtime.
commonPitfalls: Passing readonly array to mutable parameter.
Strong answer: 'Shallow compile-time. Covariant to readonly. Pair with as const.'
